sentences.text: Kentrosaurus was a small stegosaurid dinosaur discovered in the Lindi Region of Tanzania.
Adult individuals generally measured 4 to 4.5 meters in length and weighed between 700 and 1600 kilograms.
Its body featured plates that gradually merged into spikes on the hips and tail, alongside a long spike on each shoulder.
Hundreds of bones were unearthed by German expeditions in German East Africa between 1909 and 1912, with the first fossils identified as a stegosaur by Werner Janensch in 1910.
The genus was formally described by the German paleontologist Edwin Hennig in 1915, who coined the name from Greek words meaning 'sharp point' and 'lizard'.
This quadrupedal dinosaur walked on all fours with straight hindlimbs.
The longest spikes were located on the tail and were likely used for active defense.
It coexisted with carnivorous theropods like Elaphrosaurus, giant sauropods like Giraffatitan, and the dryosaurid Dysalotosaurus.
The only accepted species is Kentrosaurus aethiopicus, which serves as the type species for the genus.
Hennig originally assigned the animal to the family Stegosauridae in 1915 based on its dermal armor and angled neural spines on the tail vertebrae.
Other names, such as Kentrurosaurus and Doryphorosaurus, are now considered junior objective synonyms of Kentrosaurus.
Kentrosaurus lived in what is now Tanzania during the Late Jurassic period, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian ages.
Fossils of Kentrosaurus aethiopicus are found exclusively in the Tendaguru Formation, dated to approximately 152 million years ago.
It is debated whether the ridges on Kentrosaurus supported fleshy cheeks instead of a beak.

There is a debate over the location of a specific asymmetrical spike: classic reconstructions placed it on the hips, while recent reconstructions suggest it was on the shoulder based on comparisons with Chinese stegosaurs.
A 2025 phylogenetic analysis suggests Kentrosaurus belongs to the subfamily Dacentrurinae, though this contradicts its traditional placement in Stegosauridae.
It is debated whether the femur ratio accurately reflects sexual dimorphism because the studied specimens likely did not represent a single contemporary population.
